claim: Blood samples from 30 healthy GnRH antagonist treated males were collected at three time points: (1) before GnRH antagonist administration; (2) 3 weeks later, just before testosterone undecanoate injection, and (3) after additional 2 weeks.
source: Blood samples from 30 healthy GnRH antagonist treated males were collected at three time points: (1) before GnRH antagonist administration; (2) 3 weeks later, just before testosterone undecanoate injection, and (3) after additional 2 weeks.
evidence: This is a direct methodological statement describing the experimental design and sample collection protocol.

claim: Using receiver operating characteristic analysis, 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (4HPPD), insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 6 (IGFBP6), and fructose-bisphosphate aldolase (ALDOB) were shown to be best predictors of low (<8 nmol/l) vs normal (>12 nmol/l) testosterone.
source: Using receiver operating characteristic analysis, 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (4HPPD), insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 6 (IGFBP6), and fructose-bisphosphate aldolase (ALDOB), as well as a Multi Marker Algorithm, based on levels of 4HPPD and IGFBP6, were shown to be best predictors of low (<8 nmol/l) vs normal (>12 nmol/l) testosterone.
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis results presented in the study.

claim: A Multi Marker Algorithm based on levels of 4HPPD and IGFBP6 was shown to be a best predictor of low (<8 nmol/l) vs normal (>12 nmol/l) testosterone.
source: Using receiver operating characteristic analysis, 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (4HPPD), insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 6 (IGFBP6), and fructose-bisphosphate aldolase (ALDOB), as well as a Multi Marker Algorithm, based on levels of 4HPPD and IGFBP6, were shown to be best predictors of low (<8 nmol/l) vs normal (>12 nmol/l) testosterone.
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis results presented in the study.

claim: 4HPPD, IGFBP6, ALDOB, and Multi Marker Algorithm were more strongly associated with metabolic syndrome and diabetes than testosterone levels.
source: They were also more strongly associated with metabolic syndrome and diabetes than testosterone levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of biomarkers versus testosterone in predicting metabolic conditions.

claim: Levels of ALDOB and 4HPPD showed association with AR CAG repeat lengths.
source: Levels of ALDOB and 4HPPD also showed association with AR CAG repeat lengths.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing significant associations between protein levels and CAG repeat lengths.

claim: The male sex hormone, testosterone (T), plays an important physiological role in regulating function of both reproductive and nonreproductive organs in males as well as in females.
source: The male sex hormone, testosterone (T), plays an important physiological role in regulating function of both reproductive and nonreproductive organs in males as well as in females.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about testosterone function.

claim: The diagnosis of T deficiency (i.e., male hypogonadism) is based on the presence of low serum T levels combined with clinical symptoms, which are not pathognomonic for this condition.
source: In males, the diagnosis of T deficiency (i.e., male hypogonadism) is based on the presence of low serum T levels combined with clinical symptoms, which, however, are not pathognomonic for this condition (Traish et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Traish et al., 2011.

claim: Total T does not accurately reflect biological androgenic activity (BAA).
source: However, total T does not accurately reflect biological androgenic activity (BAA), which might be considered a more useful biological and clinical marker.
evidence: This is a statement based on established understanding in the field.

claim: The association between T levels and BAA is affected by several biological mechanisms such as the concentration of binding proteins, body mass index, certain diseases (e.g., diabetes), androgen receptor (AR) sensitivity, and different cofactors.
source: The association between T levels and BAA is affected by several biological mechanisms such as the concentration of binding proteins, body mass index, certain diseases (e.g., diabetes), androgen receptor (AR) sensitivity (Zitzmann, 2008), and different cofactors (Furuya et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zitzmann, 2008 and Furuya et al., 2013.

claim: No reliable algorithms for translating T levels into BAA are available.
source: So far, no reliable algorithms for translating T levels into BAA are available, but could be useful for example in the diagnosis of male hypogonadism.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: The symptoms associated with hypogonadism are highly nonspecific.
source: However, the treatment of men with hypogonadism represents a clinical challenge, because the symptoms associated with the condition are highly nonspecific (Miner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miner et al., 2014.

claim: In many clinical guidelines, total T concentration below 8 nmol/l indicates an insufficient hormone concentration, whereas levels above 12 nmol/l are considered normal.
source: Generally, in many clinical guidelines, total T concentration below 8 nmol/l indicates an insufficient hormone concentration, whereas levels above 12 nmol/l are considered normal (Arver and Lehtihet, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arver and Lehtihet, 2009.

claim: Low SHBG levels, as often seen in obese men, may imply low total T despite unaffected BAA.
source: Low SHBG levels, as often seen in obese men, may imply low total T despite unaffected BAA.
evidence: This is a statement based on established understanding of SHBG effects on testosterone measurements.

claim: Some degree of reduced androgen sensitivity may be associated with decreased BAA despite normal or high testosterone levels.
source: On the other hand, some degree of reduced androgen sensitivity may be associated with decreased BAA despite normal or high testosterone levels (Diaz-Arjonilla et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Diaz-Arjonilla et al., 2009.

claim: Hypogonadism has been identified as a predictor of several noncommunicable chronic diseases as well as premature mortality.
source: Hypogonadism has been identified as a predictor of several noncommunicable chronic diseases as well as premature mortality (Muraleedharan and Jones, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Muraleedharan and Jones, 2014.

claim: The first part of the study includes plasma samples obtained from 30 healthy men aged 19–32 years, BMI 19.1–26.9 kg/m2.
source: The first part of the study includes plasma samples obtained from 30 healthy men (biological replicates) aged 19–32 years, BMI 19.1–26.9 kg/m2.
evidence: This is a direct description of the study population characteristics.

claim: Subjects underwent chemical castration by subcutaneous administration of 240 mg GnRH antagonist (Degeralix, Ferring Pharmaceuticals, Saint-Prex, Switzerland) followed by remediation of testosterone levels by intramuscular injection of 1000 mg testosterone undecanoate (Nebido, Bayer AG, Leverkusen, Germany) after the duration of 3 weeks.
source: They underwent chemical castration by subcutaneous administration of 240 mg GnRH antagonist (Degeralix, Ferring Pharmaceuticals, Saint-Prex, Switzerland) followed by remediation of testosterone levels by intramuscular injection of 1000 mg testosterone undecanoate (Nebido, Bayer AG, Leverkusen, Germany) after the duration of 3 weeks (Sahlin et al., 2020; Pla et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citations to Sahlin et al., 2020 and Pla et al., 2020.

claim: A cohort of 75 serum samples from 75 men (subject age 32–43 years) previously recruited for a study on hypogonadism among men from infertile couples was used to test the clinical predictive value of the proteins identified in the castrated men.
source: To test the clinical predictive value of the proteins identified in the castrated men, we used a cohort of 75 serum samples from 75 men (biological replication, subject age 32–43 years) previously recruited for a study on hypogonadism among men from infertile couples (Bobjer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by a citation to Bobjer et al., 2016.

claim: In total, in the healthy men, the expression level of 31 out of 676 proteins was statistically significantly associated with T concentration.
source: In total, in the healthy men, the expression level of 31 out of 676 proteins was statistically significantly associated with T concentration (in Table S2 available here).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic analysis data presented in Table S2.

claim: The levels of 23 proteins changed in the same direction as T, whereas, the remaining eight markers changed in an opposite way.
source: The levels of 23 proteins changed in the same direction as T, whereas, the remaining eight markers changed in an opposite way.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of protein expression patterns in relation to testosterone levels.

claim: LH and FSH changed significantly in A and B but not in B and C.
source: LH and FSH changed significantly in A and B but not in B and C.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of hormone levels across time points.

claim: Among healthy young men, 90% of the 31 proteins distinguished the low T time point (B) from the normal ones (A and C) with statistical significance.
source: Based on p values for AUC in the ROC analysis, among healthy young men, 90% of the 31 proteins distinguished the low T time point (B) from the normal ones (A and C) with statistical significance(in Table S3 available here, Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis results presented in Table S3 and Figure 2a.

claim: ROC–AUC values greater than 0.80 were obtained for the proteins 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (4HPPD) and insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 6 (IGFBP6).
source: ROC–AUC values greater than 0.80 were obtained for the proteins 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (4HPPD) and insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 6 (IGFBP6).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis results.

claim: Fructose-bisphosphate aldolase (ALDOB) was the only protein enriched in liver tissue with ROC–AUC between 0.75 and 0.80.
source: Additionally, fructose-bisphosphate aldolase (ALDOB) was the only protein enriched in liver tissue with ROC–AUC between 0.75 and 0.80.
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis and tissue expression data.

claim: The stepwise regression method selected 4HPPD and IGFBP6 as the best markers to be combined to predict the odds of being low T.
source: The stepwise regression method selected 4HPPD and IGFBP6 as the best markers to be combined to predict the odds of being low T, and thus, they were the basis for the new variable MMA (see Material and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by stepwise regression analysis results.

claim: The expression of the 4HPPD and ALDOB proteins was significantly increased at low T (p < 0.001; p < 0.001) and remediated in response to the T treatment.
source: The expression of the 4HPPD and ALDOB proteins was significantly increasedat low T (p < 0.001; p < 0.001) and remediated in response to the T treatment, whereas IGFBP6 expression was significantly decreased (p < 0.001) by castration.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of protein expression changes across treatment conditions.

claim: IGFBP6 expression was significantly decreased (p < 0.001) by castration.
source: The expression of the 4HPPD and ALDOB proteins was significantly increasedat low T (p < 0.001; p < 0.001) and remediated in response to the T treatment, whereas IGFBP6 expression was significantly decreased (p < 0.001) by castration.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of protein expression changes.

claim: The three proteins and MMA showed statistically significant differences (4HPPD: p < 0.001, ALDOB: p = 0.003, IGFBP6: p = 0.016, MMA: p < 0.001) between the three groups defined according to the total T levels.
source: The three proteins and MMA showed statistically significant differences (4HPPD: p < 0.001, ALDOB: p = 0.003, IGFBP6: p = 0.016, MMA: p < 0.001, Figure 3a) between the three groups defined according to the total T levels (in Table S2 available here).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis results shown in Figure 3a and Table S2.

claim: 4HPPD, ALDOB, and MMA showed a negative association with T changes, while IGFBP6 displayed a positive association.
source: 4HPPD, ALDOB, and MMA showed a negative association with T changes, while IGFBP6 displayed a positive association.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of protein expression patterns in relation to testosterone levels.

claim: The three proteins and MMA significantly distinguished the patients with LT from BL_T/NT (4HPPD: AUC = 0.75, p = 0.001; ALDOB: AUC = 0.70, p = 0.008; IGFBP6: AUC = 0.69, p = 0.01; MMA: AUC = 0.79, p < 0.001).
source: The three proteins and MMA significantly distinguished the patients with LT from BL_T/NT (4HPPD: AUC = 0.75, p = 0.001; ALDOB: AUC = 0.70, p = 0.008; IGFBP6: AUC = 0.69, p = 0.01; MMA: AUC = 0.79, p < 0.001) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis results shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The power to discern low T values improved for all the biomarkers tested when the patients with BL_T were excluded.
source: Additionally, the power to discern low T values improved for all the biomarkers tested when the patients with BL_T were excluded (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative ROC analysis results shown in Table 2.

claim: The AUCs for 4HPPD, ALDOB, and MMA in relation to risk of DM and MetS were statistically significant whereas for T the p value for AUC was 0.72.
source: The AUCs for 4HPPD, ALDOB, and MMA in relation to risk of DM and MetS were statistically significant whereas for T the p value for AUC was 0.72.
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis comparing biomarkers to testosterone for predicting metabolic conditions.

claim: The AUCs for 4HPPD, ALDOB, and MMA were statistically significantly larger than this for T in predicting DM and MetS (DM: 4HPPD [p = 0.005], ALDOB [p = 0.009], MMA [p = 0.002]; MetS: 4HPPD [p = 0.032], ALDOB [p = 0.030], MMA [p = 0.002]).
source: The AUCs for 4HPPD, ALDOB, and MMA were also statistically significantly larger than this for T (DM: 4HPPD [p = 0.005], ALDOB [p = 0.009], MMA [p = 0.002]; MetS: 4HPPD [p = 0.032], ALDOB [p = 0.030], MMA [p = 0.002]; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of AUC values shown in Table 2.

claim: 4HPPD and MMA statistically significantly distinguished between patients with normal bone density and LBD.
source: 4HPPD and MMA statistically significantly distinguished between patients with normal bone density and LBD.
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis results for bone density prediction.

claim: Statistically significant inter-CAG-group overall differences were observed for 4HPPD (p = 0.012) and ALDOB (p = 0.008).
source: Statistically significant inter-CAG-group overall differences were observed for 4HPPD (p = 0.012) and ALDOB (p = 0.008) (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of protein levels across CAG repeat length groups shown in Figure 5.

claim: The protein expressions of 4HPPD and ALDOB were significantly higher in the groups with <21 and >22 CAG repeat length as compared with the reference.
source: Additionally, the protein expressions were significantly higher in the groups with <21 and >22 CAG repeat length as compared with the reference (Figure 5, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis results shown in Figure 5 and Table 3.

claim: No statistically significant association between CAG number and expression of IGFBP6 was observed.
source: However, we did not observe any statistically significant association between CAG number and expression of IGFBP6.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of IGFBP6 levels across CAG repeat length groups.

claim: ALDOB is a glycolytic enzyme, predominantly expressed in liver and kidney, that catalyzes the reversible cleavage of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and dihydroxyacetone phosphate.
source: The ALDOB is a glycolytic enzyme, predominantly expressed in liver and kidney, that catalyzes the reversible cleavage of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and dihydroxyacetone phosphate.
evidence: This is a statement of established biochemical knowledge about ALDOB function.

claim: The B isoform of aldolase, for example ALDOB, in the liver is under dietary control.
source: The B isoform of aldolase, for example ALDOB, in the liver is under dietary control (Munnich et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Munnich et al., 1985.

claim: Ingestion of fructose induces ALDOB mRNA expression in the liver, which is otherwise low in fasting conditions.
source: Ingestion of fructose induces ALDOB mRNA expression in the liver, which is otherwise low in fasting conditions.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about ALDOB regulation.

claim: In humans, the absence of functional ALDOB enzyme due to mutations in the ALDOB gene cause hereditary fructose intolerance, characterized by metabolic disturbances that include hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and hypophosphatemia.
source: In humans, the absence of functional ALDOB enzyme due to mutations in the ALDOB gene cause hereditary fructose intolerance, characterized by metabolic disturbances that include hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and hypophosphatemia (Hannou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hannou et al., 2018.

claim: An upregulation of ALDOB in human pancreatic β cells occurs upon the development of hyperglycemia and may contribute to the impairment of insulin secretion in humans.
source: An upregulation of ALDOB in human pancreatic β cells occurs upon the development of hyperglycemia and may contribute to the impairment of insulin secretion in humans (Gerst et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gerst et al., 2018.

claim: In a study on goats, the ALDOB gene was found to be downregulated at the time of postnatal initiation of spermatogenesis.
source: In a study on goats, the ALDOB gene was found to be downregulated at the time of postnatal initiation of spermatogenesis (Bo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bo et al., 2020.

claim: 4HPPD is involved in the catabolic pathway of tyrosine and catalyzes the conversion of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate to homogentisic acid in the tyrosine catabolism pathway.
source: This enzyme is involved in the catabolic pathway of tyrosine and catalyzes the conversion of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate to homogentisic acid in the tyrosine catabolism pathway (Hager et al., 1957).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hager et al., 1957.

claim: The expression of the 4HPPD gene is regulated by hepatocyte-specific and liver-enriched transcription factors, as well as by hormones.
source: The expression of the gene is regulated by hepatocyte-specific and liver-enriched transcription factors, as well as by hormones (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2014.

claim: Tyrosine has previously been reported to be upregulated in hypogonadal men and both tyrosine and phenylalanine levels were suggested as predictors of the risk of developing diabetes many years before manifest disease.
source: Tyrosine has previously been reported to be upregulated in hypogonadal men and both tyrosine and phenylalanine levels were suggested as predictors of the risk of developing diabetes many years before manifest disease (Wang et al., 2011; Fanelli et al., 2018; Guasch-Ferré et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2011; Fanelli et al., 2018; Guasch-Ferré et al., 2016.

claim: In male tyrosine hydroxylase knockout mice normal body weight, puberty onset, and basal gonadotropin levels in adulthood were evident, although T was significantly elevated in adult mice.
source: In male tyrosine hydroxylase knockout mice normal body weight, puberty onset, and basal gonadotropin levels in adulthood were evident, although T was significantly elevated in adult mice (Stephens et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stephens et al., 2017.

claim: IGFBP6 is expressed in most tissues.
source: The last marker, IGFBP6 is expressed in most tissues (Kim et al., 2014) and is one of the binding proteins for insulin-like growth factor (IGF).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2014.

claim: IGFBP6 is one of the binding proteins for insulin-like growth factor (IGF).
source: The last marker, IGFBP6 is expressed in most tissues (Kim et al., 2014) and is one of the binding proteins for insulin-like growth factor (IGF).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about IGFBP6 function.

claim: The principal function of IGFBP6 is inhibiting IGF-II actions, whereby IGF-II-induced cell proliferation, differentiation, migration, and survival is reduced.
source: The principal function of IGFBP6 is inhibiting IGF-II actions, whereby IGF-II-induced cell proliferation, differentiation, migration, and survival is reduced.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about IGFBP6 function.

claim: Serum levels of IGFBP6 increase gradually with age and are higher in men than in women.
source: Serum levels of IGFBP6 increase gradually with age and are higher in men than in women, but there are conflicting studies of the direct effects of sex steroids on IGFBP6 expression in different tissues (Bach et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bach et al., 2013.

claim: A positive association between the levels of T and IGFBP6 have previously been found.
source: A positive association between the levels of T and IGFBP6 have previously been found (Rooman et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rooman et al., 2005 and Huang et al., 2019.

claim: Early increases in IGFBP6 levels in men receiving testosterone were associated with increases in fat-free mass and muscle strength.
source: The study showed that early increases in IGFBP6 levels in men receiving testosterone were associated with increases in fat-free mass and muscle strength.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from a cited study (Huang et al., 2019).

claim: The combined parameter MMA may be an important tool in the detection of long-term morbidity, such as bone mineral density and cardiometabolic risk, even before clinical diagnosis.
source: However, our findings cannot be used as a direct proof of hypogonadism being cause of cardiometabolic disease but the combined parameter MMA may in this context be an important tool in the detection of long-term morbidity, such as bone mineral density and cardiometabolic risk, even before clinical diagnosis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical utility based on the study findings.

claim: 87% of FDA-approved biomarkers are in the same concentration range as the more than 450 proteins identified in this study.
source: We were able to identify more than 450 proteins, which were identified in the same concentration range as 87% of FDA-approved biomarkers (Anderson, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2010.

claim: The proteins removed by depletion are of highest abundance in plasma and plasma proteome and exceed some lower abundance proteins by 10 orders of magnitude.
source: If depletion is not performed the detection level is dampened by the components from the digested abundant proteins as the proteins removed are of highest abundance in plasma and plasma proteome and exceed some lower abundance proteins by 10 orders of magnitude (Tu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tu et al., 2010.

claim: Median length CAG number is associated with most active AR.
source: We have previously shown that median length CAG number is associated with most active AR (Nenonen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nenonen et al., 2010.

claim: The fact that the lowest ALDOB and 4HPPD levels are found in subjects having AR CAG repeat length close to median confirms that the candidate markers identified in the present study are androgen dependent.
source: Thus, the fact that we find the lowest ALDOB and 4HPPD levels in those subjects having AR CAG repeat length close to median, confirms thatthe candidate markers identified in the present study are androgen dependent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the association between CAG repeat length and protein levels.

claim: In the concentration range seen in males, there seems to be high correlation between concentration values obtained by immunoassay and by LC–MS/MS.
source: Additionally, in the concentration range seen in males, there seems to be high correlation between concentration values obtained by immunoassay and by LC–MS/MS (Huhtaniemi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huhtaniemi et al., 2012.

claim: In identifying men in hypogonadal T range and prediction of cardiometabolic risk, assessment of T by LC–MS/MS was not shown to be superior to that performed by standard methodology.
source: Also in identifying men in hypogonadal T range and prediction of cardiometabolic risk, assessment of T by LC–MS/MS was not shown to be superior to that performed by standard methodology (Huhtaniemi et al., 2012; Haring et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huhtaniemi et al., 2012 and Haring et al., 2013.

claim: Meta-analysis of 12 cohort studies demonstrated significantly increased risk of osteoporotic fractures for men at z-scores ≤ −1 SD.
source: The rationale is based primarily on meta-analysis of 12 cohort studies demonstrating significantly increased risk of osteoporotic fractures for men at z-scores ≤ −1 SD (Johnell et al., 2005) and in addition because it has also been shown that the majority of fragility fractures occur in patients with BMD in the osteopenic range, that is T-score between −1 and −2.5. (Unnanuntana et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Johnell et al., 2005.

claim: The majority of fragility fractures occur in patients with BMD in the osteopenic range, that is T-score between −1 and −2.5.
source: The rationale is based primarily on meta-analysis of 12 cohort studies demonstrating significantly increased risk of osteoporotic fractures for men at z-scores ≤ −1 SD (Johnell et al., 2005) and in addition because it has also been shown that the majority of fragility fractures occur in patients with BMD in the osteopenic range, that is T-score between −1 and −2.5. (Unnanuntana et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Unnanuntana et al., 2010.

source: The work was supported by ReproUnion2.0 (grant no. 20201846), which is funded by the Interreg V EU program.
evidence: This is a direct statement about funding sources.

claim: The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD024448.
source: The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE (Perez-Riverol et al., 2019) partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD024448.
